request.system: You are an expert in clinical classification systems.

messages.content:
ICD-10-AM is the Australian modification of the International Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems, 10th revision. Its disease codes are arranged in chapters, and a three-character category is written as one capital letter followed by two digits. The letter indicates the chapter or block: A and B are infectious diseases, C is malignant neoplasms, D is other neoplasms and blood disorders, E is endocrine, nutritional and metabolic disease, F is mental and behavioural disorders, G is the nervous system, H is the eye and ear, I is the circulatory system, J is the respiratory system, K is the digestive system, L is the skin, M is the musculoskeletal system, N is the genitourinary system, O is pregnancy and childbirth, P is the perinatal period, Q is congenital malformations, R is symptoms and abnormal findings, S and T are injury and poisoning, and Z is factors influencing health status. The two digits narrow the chapter to a specific category, for example J44 is chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and N17 is acute kidney failure.

The principal diagnosis is the single condition established after investigation to be chiefly responsible for the patient's episode of admitted care. It is not the patient's most serious comorbidity, not the presenting symptom, and not the procedure performed.

Using that structure, assign the three-character ICD-10-AM principal diagnosis category for the episode below. Choose the chapter letter first, then the two digits.

Hospital course:
Discharge Summary:

Patient Name: [redacted]
Medical Record Number: [redacted]
Date of Discharge: [redacted]

Admission Date: [redacted]
Chief Complaint: Severe substernal chest pain and diaphoresis
Final Diagnosis: [diagnosis section withheld]
Hospital Course:
The patient, a 38-year-old male with a past medical history of high blood pressure, high cholesterol, and HIV infection, presented to the ED with severe chest pain and sweating. He had been having intermittent chest pain for one month that was worsened by exercise and heavy lifting and was not relieved by medication.
The physical examination was unremarkable except for elevated levels of troponin-I and ST-segment elevation on ECG, suggesting an inferior wall myocardial infarction (IWMI). The patient was immediately transferred to the cardiac catheterization laboratory for an emergent coronary angiogram procedure, which revealed an LAD wrapped around the apex with 95% stenosis.
Balloon angioplasty was successfully performed, and a drug-eluting stent was placed in the 95% lesion of the LAD with minimal residual stenosis. The patient remained stable in the post-operative period and was discharged on aspirin, atorvastatin, metoprolol, enalapril, and ticagrelor, which were prescribed to manage his condition.

Hospital Course Summary:
The patient was admitted to the ED with severe substernal chest pain and sweating, which was diagnosed as an impending STEMI. After being treated with an emergent coronary angiogram procedure, balloon angioplasty, and a drug-eluting stent, the patient remained stable and was discharged with medications to control his condition.

Answer in the form CODE: <letter><digit><digit>

text:
CODE: I21

The episode is an acute inferior wall myocardial infarction (elevated troponin-I and ST elevation on ECG), treated with emergent angiography, angioplasty, and stenting. That places it in the circulatory chapter (I) under acute myocardial infarction (I21). The summary's "impending STEMI" wording is less definitive than the body of the notes, which document an infarction.
